newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda says will retaliate against Sudan air raid.
newsitem.headline: Uganda says will retaliate against Sudan air raid.

text.p: Uganda said on Monday it would retaliate against a bombing raid by Sudanese warplanes on northern Uganda in contravention of a peace agreement the two countries forged this month.

Minister of State for Defence Amama Mbabazi said two Sudanese MiG planes on Sunday dropped bombs aimed at an army barracks in the northwestern town of Moyo, 16 km (10 miles) south of Sudan's border. He said the bombs missed their target.
"It is true we have been bombed by Sudan...It is surprising that even before the ink dries on the agreement we signed they are bombing us," Mbabazi told reporters.
"We shall not sit back and watch while our territory continues to be violated. We shall soon respond appropriately."

Under the September 9 pact, mediated by Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani on a visit to Khartoum and Kampala, the two countries agreed to work to halt activity by rebels in the border area. Both accuse each other of supporting rebel groups.
Sunday's air raid was the first since Sudanese planes bombed northern Uganda in January in an attack Khartoum said was aimed against southern Sudanese rebels.
"Two Sudanese MiGs came over on Sunday and dropped a number of bombs, around 10. Not all fell on Moyo and we have no reports of casualties," an aid worker, who declined to be named, told Reuters.

Other aid workers said they heard from the region that the MiGs attacked at 9:30 a.m. and dropped bombs and fired rockets at Moyo but no reports of casualties or damage were received, possibly as there were no aid agencies in the immediate area.
Sudan and Uganda had agreed to move any refugees and "hostile elements" at least 100 km (60 miles) from their common border, and to encourage voluntary repatriation of refugees.
The main southern Sudanese rebel group, the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), had refused to comment on the pact.

But on Monday SPLA Information Secretary Pa'gan Amum told Reuters: "The raid on Sunday is no surprise in as much as...the agreement is not working and will not work because Khartoum is an expanisionist force and will not abide by any agreement."
He said the SPLA had no presence in Uganda so the raid was apparently a move by Khartoum to act in support of the Ugandan rebel West Nile Bank Front, which is active in the Moyo region.

The leader of the main Sudanese opposition alliance, based in Eritrea, had dismissed the pact as meaningless. Mubarak al-Mahdi, secretary-general of the National Democratic Alliance, said he had no faith it would work as there was no confidence between the Ugandan and Sudanese governments.
He said he believed Khartoum would keep supplying arms to rebels of the Lord's Resistance Army (LRA) fighting in northern Uganda and the SPLA would continue to have good ties to Kampala.
The LRA denies being armed by Khartoum and the SPLA denies being backed by Kampala.
The September 9 pact aimed at stopping the LRA taking refuge in southern Sudan and the SPLA taking refuge in northern Uganda.

Ugandan officials said there was no provision in the agreement for both countries to restore relations but said it included a foreign verification team to monitor the border area. Uganda broke relations with Sudan in April last year.
The SPLA has fought for greater autonomy or the independence of the mainly Christian and animist south of Sudan from the Moslem, Arabised north since 1983.
